title: Question 4
stem:
A child moves down a long slide, as shown in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1 (not to scale)

The child moves from rest at the top end $X$ of the slide. An average resistive force of $76\text{ N}$ opposes the motion of the child as they move to the lower end $Y$ of the slide. The kinetic energy of the child at $Y$ is $300\text{ J}$. The decrease in gravitational potential energy of the child as it moves from $X$ to $Y$ is $3200\text{ J}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Determine the ratio

$$\frac{\text{kinetic energy of the child at Y when the resistive force is 76 N}}{\text{kinetic energy of the child at Y if there is no resistive force}}$$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about energy conservation first - if there were no friction at all, what would all the lost gravitational potential energy have turned into at Y?
parts.proper_answer: With no resistive force, $KE = 3200\text{ J}$. Ratio $= 300/3200 = 0.094$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What happens with no friction?**
You start at X with no speed, so you have only gravitational potential energy. As you slide down you lose $3200\text{ J}$ of that. With nothing opposing you, every joule of that must appear as kinetic energy at Y. So ideal $KE = 3200\text{ J}$.

Step 2: **Form the ratio**
The real $KE$ with friction is only $300\text{ J}$. So: $$\text{ratio} = \frac{300}{3200} = 0.09375 \approx 0.094$$ It has no unit because joules cancel.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Use the answer in (a) to calculate the ratio

$$\frac{\text{speed of the child at Y when the resistive force is 76 N}}{\text{speed of the child at Y if there is no resistive force}}$$.
hints: Hint 1: Recall how kinetic energy depends on speed - it is not linear, so the speed ratio will not be the same as the energy ratio from (a).
Hint 2: Since mass cancels in a ratio, the speed ratio is the square root of the energy ratio you just found.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link energy to speed**
For the same child of mass $m$, kinetic energy is: $$KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ That means $v^2$ is proportional to $KE$, or $v$ is proportional to $\sqrt{KE}$. A common slip is to use the energy ratio directly for speed - you must take the square root.

Step 2: **Apply to the ratio**
Mass $m$ and $1/2$ are the same in top and bottom, so they cancel: $$\frac{v_{with}}{v_{without}} = \sqrt{\frac{KE_{with}}{KE_{without}}} = \sqrt{0.09375}$$ $$\approx 0.31$$ So the speed is reduced to about one third, even though the energy is reduced to less than one tenth.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Calculate the length of the slide from $X$ to $Y$.
hints: Hint 1: Start with an energy balance - the missing energy between the 3200 J lost and the 300 J gained as kinetic energy must have gone into work against friction.
Hint 2: Remember work done by a constant force is force times distance along the slope, so you can find the slide length from that missing energy and the 76 N force.
parts.proper_answer: Work against friction $= 3200 - 300 = 2900\text{ J}$. Length $= 2900/76 = 38\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the energy lost to friction**
Energy is conserved overall, just spread out. Lost $GPE$ = useful $KE$ + work against friction: $$3200 = 300 + W$$ So $$W = 3200 - 300 = 2900\text{ J}$$ This is the thermal and sound energy produced by rubbing along the slide.

Step 2: **Convert work to distance**
For a constant resistive force along the direction of motion: $$W = F \times d$$ Rearrange before putting numbers in: $$d = \frac{W}{F} = \frac{2900}{76}$$ $$d \approx 38\text{ m}$$ That is the length from X to Y along the slope.

parts.label: (d)
parts.part_stem: A spring connects the board to a fixed point. The spring obeys Hooke's law and has a spring constant of $63\text{ N m}^{-1}$. The child hits the board so that it moves to the right and compresses the spring. The speed of the child becomes zero when the elastic potential energy of the spring has increased to its maximum value of $140\text{ J}$.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the maximum compression of the spring.

markscheme_points.text: E = ½kx 2 or E = ½Fx and F = kx 140 = ½ × 63 × x 2 or 140 = ½Fx and F = 63x

hints: Hint 1: The spring stores energy when compressed - recall the formula linking elastic energy to spring constant $k$ and compression $x$.
Hint 2: You know the stored energy is 140 J and $k = 63\text{ N m}^{-1}$, so rearrange that energy formula to make $x$ the subject before substituting.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the spring energy law**
For a spring obeying Hooke's law, the elastic potential energy for compression $x$ is: $$E = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$$ This is the area under the $F$-$x$ graph where $F = kx$. Here $E = 140\text{ J}$ and $k = 63\text{ N m}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Solve for compression**
Rearrange first: $$x = \sqrt{\frac{2E}{k}}$$ Then substitute: $$x = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 140}{63}} = \sqrt{\frac{280}{63}}$$ $$x \approx 2.1\text{ m}$$ That is the maximum compression when the child momentarily stops.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of the transfer of the kinetic energy of the child to the elastic potential energy of the spring.
hints: Hint 1: Efficiency always compares useful output energy to input energy - identify which two energies from the story are the input kinetic energy at Y and the output spring energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply efficiency**
The child arrives with $300\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy. Only $140\text{ J}$ ends up stored in the spring, the rest is lost in the impact and as heat and sound. Efficiency is: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{input}} \times 100$$ $$= \frac{140}{300} \times 100 \approx 47\%$$

parts.label: (d)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about the shape given by $E = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ - how does a squared relationship look on a graph starting at zero?
Hint 2: Consider what the gradient represents and how the spring force $F = kx$ changes as $x$ grows, to decide if the curve gets steeper or shallower.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at origin with increasing positive gradient (parabola) from $x = 0$ to $x = x_0$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise the x-squared shape**
Since $E = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$, energy is proportional to $x^2$, not $x$. So the graph is not a straight line. It must start at $(0,0)$ because zero compression means zero stored energy, and curve upwards.

Step 2: **Why the gradient increases**
The gradient of an $E$-$x$ graph is force, and Hooke's law says $F = kx$ grows with $x$. So as you compress more, each extra mm stores more energy than the last. Draw a smooth parabola-like curve from the origin to $x_0$ that gets steeper and steeper.
